note: Draws lessons from aerospace and pharmaceutical safety evaluation, which is the professional model an AI audit practice is working toward.
title: Toward an Evaluation Science for Generative AI Systems
explain_beginner: The paper argues that today's methods for checking generative AI are not good enough. Fixed test sets may not show how a system behaves in real use, and single reviews cannot cover everything at scale. It looks at how other safety critical fields, such as transport, aerospace, and pharmaceutical safety, built their evaluation practices. From them it draws three lessons. Tests should measure performance in actual use, they should be improved repeatedly, and there should be organizations and shared rules around evaluation. This matters because better evaluation can help people understand and prepare for how generative AI performs before and during deployment.
explain_business: For executives, the paper warns that relying only on fixed tests or single reviews may give an incomplete picture of generative AI in real operations. It recommends building stronger evaluation practices, using lessons from mature safety fields like transport, aerospace, and pharmaceuticals. In practice, teams should track whether metrics match real use, update them as systems and contexts change, and support shared standards and oversight. This informs decisions about when and how to deploy generative AI, what evidence to require before use, and how much to trust current evaluation results. It suggests treating evaluation as a continuing need, not a single check.
explain_practitioner: The paper argues that current evaluation practice for generative AI is inadequate. Fixed test sets often do not establish that results transfer to real use, while single audits do not scale. To address this, the authors examine safety testing in transport, aerospace, and pharmaceuticals and derive three lessons for generative AI. Metrics should reflect performance in actual use, they should be revised repeatedly, and evaluation needs supporting organizations and shared rules. The paper then sketches a route toward a more disciplined evaluation field. Its main contribution is this framework and direction, not a new model, test, or empirical result.
